headline: The Lens Blur Fix That Separates Polished Demos From Loom Slop
lede: Founders routinely undercut first impressions by shipping raw screen recordings when a small investment in post-production could close what practitioners call the 'polish gap.' Derek Feehrer — co-founder of Kite, a Y Combinator-backed screen-recording tool — argues the gap is visible to everyone, including people too polite to say so. The technique he is promoting: simulating the shallow depth-of-field look of a film camera, applied to software demos.
body:
The effect Feehrer describes — **cinematic lens blur** — borrows from cinematography's *shallow depth of field* principle, where a wide-aperture lens keeps the foreground subject sharp while the background dissolves into smooth *bokeh*. Applied to a screen recording, the active application window stays in crisp focus while the desktop environment — wallpaper, dock, notification badges — blurs softly behind it. The result mimics product photography and signals intentionality to a viewer who may not consciously notice the effect but will feel it.

The critique of Loom is pointed but not entirely unfair. Loom — acquired by Atlassian (TEAM) for $975 million in November 2023 — was designed for asynchronous internal communication: quick recordings for teammates who already share context. Its free tier caps resolution at 720p and stamps a watermark on every video. It lacks auto-zoom, motion blur, or cinematic backgrounds. Using it for an investor demo or landing page is a category error: the format signals 'internal update' when the message should be 'trust this product.'

A cottage industry of tools has grown to fill the gap. Screen Studio, a bootstrapped macOS app built by indie developer Adam Pietrasiak, became a cult favorite by automating smooth cursor movement and zoom-on-click, winning #1 Product of the Year on Product Hunt. FocuSee, made by iMobie, offers cross-platform 3D depth-of-field simulation. Kite — Feehrer's own company — goes furthest: its AI adds 3D device mockups, kinetic text scenes, and AI voiceovers with minimal manual input. For founders who prefer granular control, CapCut's Lens Blur effect and Adobe (ADBE) After Effects' Camera Lens Blur tool can approximate the look in two or three manual steps.

The stakes are real. Startup marketing research suggests polished demo videos can lift landing-page conversion by two to four times, and Y Combinator partners have noted they frequently watch a 60-second product demo before engaging with a slide deck. An unpolished recording doesn't just look amateurish; it signals that the founder hasn't thought carefully about the viewer's first encounter with the product.

Feehrer is not a disinterested observer. Kite is almost certainly what he is linking to when he promises a '2-minute' fix, and the ease of that promise assumes Kite's one-click automation rather than a manual CapCut workflow. Still, the core observation stands independent of any tool: in a landscape where early-stage products are increasingly discovered through short video, the cheapest credibility signal available to a founder may simply be better production value.

concepts.definition: A post-production effect applied to screen recordings that simulates the look of a wide-aperture film camera. The primary subject — the application window — stays sharp while surrounding desktop elements blur into a smooth haze, mimicking the shallow depth-of-field look associated with professional product video.

A cinematographic term for the effect produced by a wide-aperture (low f-stop) lens, where only a narrow plane of the scene is in focus and objects in front of or behind it blur. In software demos it is simulated in post-production rather than captured in-camera.

From the Japanese word for 'blur' or 'haze.' In photography and video, it refers to the aesthetic quality of the out-of-focus areas in an image — typically smooth, rounded blurs of background light. It is closely associated with shallow depth-of-field and is considered a mark of professional cinematography.

A communication format popularized by Loom, where the sender records a video message and recipients watch it on their own schedule rather than meeting live. Built for internal team use, it trades visual polish for speed and convenience — a reasonable bargain for a quick team update, a poor one for an external product demo.

A feature in polished screen recording tools that automatically zooms the camera toward wherever the presenter clicks or interacts, guiding the viewer's eye without manual editing. Absent from raw Loom recordings; present in tools like Screen Studio and Kite.

The observable difference in perceived quality between a raw, unedited screen recording and one processed with cinematic effects, motion design, and post-production. In the startup context it specifically describes the impression gap between utilitarian tools like Loom and dedicated demo-video platforms.

fact_check: The '2-minute' claim is presented as a general, tool-agnostic technique, but the ease almost certainly depends on Kite — Feehrer's own product — rather than a universal method. A manual CapCut or After Effects lens-blur workflow takes longer and requires more technical comfort. The tweet also omits the self-promotional dimension: it is, in effect, advertising Kite without identifying it as such.
